title: Where should a COO start with AI?
description: Where AI helps operations first, who keeps the calls, what to measure, and a one-page brief for your CEO. Built on Census, BLS and field studies.
verdict: AI helps most with answering, drafting and compiling around operations, not with directing it.[^10][^1]
Gains come from redesigning one workflow, not from buying seats.[^16][^17]
People keep the calls, and the firm owns what its AI tells customers.[^29][^23]
Expect a few percent of hours saved at first, so measure against a baseline.[^8][^9]
Larger firms use AI more: about a third of firms with 100 to 249 staff did by May 2026.[^2][^1]

onPage.text: Which calls your planners, controller and service leads keep
Six ops jobs where AI pays first, with the number to measure
Straight answers to what your CEO or board will ask
A one-page brief you can forward to your CEO
Three 90-day starts, sized to your firm
Our analysis of which ops jobs AI helps, and with which part

headings.what-it-is: What is AI for operations, and what does it change?
headings.decisions: Which AI decisions does a COO own?
headings.ranked: Where does AI pay first in operations?
headings.faq: What will your CEO or board ask?
headings.what-goes-wrong: Where does AI in operations go wrong?
headings.buy-or-build: Should you buy AI for operations or build it?

answers.human-role: Your people keep every call that directs, schedules or commits the firm. AI drafts, answers and flags work for them to check.[^10][^29]
answers.decisions: A COO owns six AI calls: what to fix first, who checks output, redesign or bolt-on, saved time, buy or build, and which tools staff may use.[^15][^29]
answers.ranked: AI pays first on customer and order questions, then order paperwork and status writing, where field studies show the biggest gains.[^3][^4]
answers.faq: Your CEO or board will ask about jobs, payback, ownership, tools already bought, peers and data safety.[^13][^15]
answers.recipes: A 90-day start is one workflow, four weeks of baseline, six weeks of pilot against a hold-out group, then a keep, change or stop call.[^3][^6]
answers.benchmark: Show it worked by comparing a pilot group with a hold-out group against four weeks of baseline, then pricing the gain in dollars.[^3][^6]
answers.what-goes-wrong: AI in operations goes wrong when pilots lack an owner, agents are oversold, customers get wrong answers or nobody checks the output.[^20][^22]
answers.something-else: Pick something else when the process is broken, the rules are fixed, the problem is a forecast, or physical work dominates.[^16][^10]

summary: AI for operations means tools that read, write, answer and sort the paperwork around your operation, while your people keep the calls.[^1][^10] AI speeds up answering, drafting and checking, not who decides.[^3] Whether it pays depends on redesigning the workflow, not on buying seats.[^16][^17]
humanRole: COO: owns the risk call and the list of AI outputs that need a human check.[^29][^30] High performers set rules for when people must validate AI output.[^15]
Customer service lead: approves every answer pattern before AI uses it with customers, and owns the route to a person. A tribunal held Air Canada liable for its chatbot's wrong advice.[^23]
Planner or scheduler: keeps the schedule and work assignments, while AI drafts and flags. In our analysis, scheduling and assigning work show no measurable AI use.[^10][^11]
Controller: signs off any AI-matched or AI-coded number before it posts.[^30] On a task outside AI's range, AI users were 19 points less likely to be right.[^5]

decisions.know: Which roles spend most time answering, drafting and compiling, and today's cost per unit.[^10][^32] Most AI-using firms start in three or fewer of 15 functions.[^1]

decisions.decision: Who owns each workflow, and who checks output
decisions.know: Senior leaders at AI high performers are three times as likely to show ownership.[^15] NIST, the US standards agency, asks for defined human oversight roles.[^29][^30]

decisions.decision: Redesign the workflow, or bolt on a tool
decisions.know: Of 25 traits surveyed, redesign had the biggest effect on earnings (EBIT), yet only 21% of organizations using generative AI had done it.[^16] Another found redesign made measurable gains 24 points more likely.[^17]

decisions.decision: What staff do with time saved
decisions.know: Two in three frontline users get limited or no guidance on using saved time.[^17] Gains were 10% to 40% larger where employers encouraged use.[^7]

Firms now buy 76% of their AI use cases, up from 53%, say enterprise AI decision-makers polled by Menlo Ventures, an AI investor.[^31] Bought or partnered tools reached deployment about twice as often as internal builds.[^20]
Over half of workers, 54%, would use AI tools even if not authorized.[^18] In 6.8% of firms, staff use AI though the firm has not adopted it.[^1]

ranked.name: Customer and order questions
ranked.why: Customer service reps rank 7th of 785 jobs for AI help in our analysis.[^10] Support agents with an AI assistant resolved 14% more issues an hour, and novices about 34% more.[^3]
ranked.payoff: Resolutions per hour, escalations and new-hire ramp time.

ranked.name: Order entry and order-to-cash paperwork
ranked.why: Median order-to-cash takes 38 days and costs $2.32 per $1,000 of revenue, per APQC, a benchmarking body.[^34][^35] A vendor-sponsored 2017 survey of 167 supply chain and customer service representatives found automated order entry cut cycle time over 46%.[^36]
ranked.payoff: Order entry hours, error rate and days to invoice.

ranked.name: Status updates, reports and email
ranked.why: Professionals using ChatGPT finished writing tasks 40% faster at 18% higher quality.[^4] Copilot users spent about 2 fewer hours a week on email.[^6]
ranked.payoff: Hours a week on email and reports, and report turnaround.

ranked.name: Purchase orders and supplier questions
ranked.why: APQC's median cost to process a purchase order is $55, and issuing one takes 2.0 days.[^32][^33] AI helps buyers gather product facts, but negotiating shows no AI use.[^10]
ranked.payoff: Cost per purchase order and days to issue one.

ranked.name: Records, reconciliations and data checks
ranked.why: Compiling records scores high for AI help, but reconciling financial data shows no use in our analysis.[^10] So AI prepares and flags, and people keep the matching rules and sign-off.[^30]
ranked.payoff: Exceptions per close and days to close.

ranked.name: Planning and forecasting
ranked.why: A 2026 operations survey finds planning and sourcing lead AI use.[^19] Chat tools show no use for analyzing data to improve operations, so this pays through a forecasting model.[^10]
ranked.payoff: Forecast error against last year's method.

faq.q: Will AI replace our operations managers?
faq.a: No: the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) projects operations manager jobs to grow 5.0% from 2025 to 2035, above 3.5% for all jobs.[^13] BLS rates the role high for AI exposure, but says exposure does not imply job loss.[^14] In our analysis, 69% of the role's work shows no AI use.[^10]

faq.q: What's the return on AI, and when will we see it?
faq.a: Expect returns per workflow first, not company-wide: only 39% of firms report any EBIT impact from AI.[^15] Users save about 5.4% of their hours, or 2.2% of all work hours.[^8][^9] So set a baseline and judge each workflow at day 90.

faq.q: Who owns AI here, the COO or IT?
faq.a: The workflow owner owns the result, and IT owns access and security.[^30] NIST puts AI risk decisions with executive leadership.[^29] Senior leaders at AI high performers show ownership three times as often.[^15]

faq.q: Why did the AI tools we bought change nothing?
faq.a: Seats without a redesigned workflow rarely move the numbers.[^16][^17] Only 21% of firms using generative AI had redesigned any workflow, the step with the biggest earnings effect.[^16] In a Copilot field study, email time fell but the mix of tasks did not change.[^6]

faq.q: Are firms our size using AI yet?
faq.a: Yes: 32% of US firms with 100 to 249 staff and 37% with 250 or more used AI, in Census data to 3 May 2026.[^2] The national rate was 19.8%, and use rose among firms with 20 or more staff.[^2][^1]

faq.q: Is our data safe in these tools?
faq.a: Only on business plans with admin controls, plus a written list of allowed tools.[^39][^18] Google says Workspace data isn't used to train its models; that is the vendor's claim.[^39] A 2025 survey found 54% of workers would use unapproved tools anyway.[^18]

forward: Top workflow: customer and order questions. Support agents with AI resolved 14% more issues an hour.[^3][^10]
What it saves: writing and email time first, about 40% on writing tasks.[^4][^6] Expect a few percent of total hours, not a step change.[^8][^9]
Risk and who checks: the firm owns what its AI tells customers.[^23] The ops lead approves answer patterns, and the controller signs off numbers.
First step: one workflow, four weeks of baseline, then a pilot against a hold-out group.[^3][^6]
Cost: AI seats list at $14 to $21 a user a month, so by our math 15 users for 90 days cost at most $945.[^39][^37] Connecting AI to your order or ticket system costs extra.
How we'll know: resolutions per hour, order cycle time and cost per purchase order, against APQC medians of 38 days and $55.[^34][^32]

recipes.name: 1. Small ops team, about 40 to 100 staff: seat tools plus one workflow
recipes.when: No IT team, and Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace already in place. Most firms start AI in three or fewer functions.[^1]
flow: COO: pick one workflow, such as order status emails or the weekly ops report, and name an owner (days 1 to 10)
Ops lead: record four weeks of baseline: volume, hours, error rate and turnaround
Office manager or IT admin: turn on business-plan seats for 10 to 15 users and post the allowed-tools list
Ops lead: write answer templates and a check-before-send rule, then train users
Ops lead: run six weeks with a hold-out group and compare
COO: keep, change or stop at day 90
recipes.cost: Copilot Business lists at $21 a user a month, annual; ChatGPT Business at $20; Google Business Standard at $14 (read 26 Nov 2026).[^37][^38][^39] Fifteen users for three months at $21 is $945 in seats.

recipes.name: 2. Mid-size firm, 100 to 500 staff: service desk assist
recipes.when: A service or inside-sales team of 10 or more answering repeat questions. Novice agents gained most in the field study.[^3]
flow: COO: sponsor the pilot and set the measures: resolutions per hour and escalations
Customer service lead: build an approved answer library from past tickets
IT: connect the AI assistant to the ticketing system and knowledge base
Agents: AI suggests replies, and agents edit and send; no auto-send in the first 90 days
Quality lead: check 5% to 10% of AI-assisted replies each week for accuracy
COO: compare gains for new and experienced agents at day 90
recipes.cost: Seat prices as in recipe 1.[^37][^38] We did not check helpdesk AI add-on prices, so ask your helpdesk vendor for its list price.

recipes.name: 3. Document-heavy operation: orders or invoices arrive as PDFs
recipes.when: Orders or invoices arrive by email and get retyped into your ERP (enterprise resource planning system). APQC's median purchase order costs $55 to process.[^32]
flow: COO: pick the document flow with the highest volume
Order desk or accounts payable lead: count documents, minutes each and error rate for four weeks
IT or integrator: set up extraction into the ERP with a review queue
Order desk lead: approve every low-confidence field and track the exception rate
Controller: sign off the posting rules
COO: compare cost per order with the baseline and APQC's median
recipes.cost: We give no list price here; our document processing and invoice processing guides carry their own price checks. Measure against your baseline and APQC's medians.[^32][^35]

ownData.title: Which jobs in your operation does AI help most, and with which part?
ownData.intro: AI helps customer service reps and order clerks most, with answering and explaining; directing, scheduling, assigning and negotiating show no AI use.[^10][^11] We calculated these shares on 26 Nov 2026 from Microsoft Research's public Working with AI data, licensed CC BY 4.0.[^10][^11] Jobs and pay come from BLS, May 2025.[^12]
headers: Work with no AI use seen
ownData.note: Method: we weight each job's activities by importance; help is completion times scope in about 200,000 US Bing Copilot chats from 2024. A lot means a help score of 0.40 or more; no use seen means too few chats to measure, not that AI can't help. Limits: consumer chats, not your firm's tools; scores show current use, not job loss, for the US with no firm-size cut.

howToTest: Pick one workflow and one unit: a ticket, order, purchase order or report. Record four weeks of volume, minutes per unit, errors and cycle time.
Compare your baseline with outside medians: APQC's 38-day order-to-cash, $55 per purchase order and 2.0 days to issue one.[^34][^32][^33]
Split users into a pilot group with AI and a hold-out group without, on similar work. Both big field studies measured AI users against non-users.[^3][^6]
Measure quality as well as speed. Consultants using AI were faster and better inside AI's range, but 19 points less accurate outside it.[^5]
Check self-reported time savings against system data. In an early-2025 trial, developers were 19% slower with AI while believing they were 20% faster.[^26]
Count rework that lands on others. In a survey with BetterUp, a coaching vendor, 40% of desk workers had received AI work needing fixes in the past month.[^24][^25]
Track where saved time goes. Danish workers moved 80% of saved time to other tasks.[^7]

Price the lift: share of a role's year saved times annual pay, plus errors avoided, minus seats and setup. Example: by our math, 5% of a customer service rep's year at the BLS annual mean wage of $46,590 is about $2,330.[^12]
Decide at day 90: keep, change or stop.
watchOuts: Pilots that never ship: an MIT study found 95% of firms saw no measurable profit impact from generative AI.[^20][^21] Fix: one workflow, one owner, a baseline and a day-90 decision.

Agent hype: Gartner expects over 40% of agentic AI projects to be canceled by end of 2027, and warns of agent washing.[^22] Fix: demand a demo on your own documents, and start with assist, not autonomy.
Wrong answers to customers: Air Canada was held liable for its chatbot, and Klarna said a cost focus cut quality.[^23][^27][^28] Fix: a person approves answer patterns, with an easy route to staff.
Using AI outside what it does well: on such a task, consultants with AI were 19 points less likely to be right.[^5] Fix: test your own hard cases before rollout.
Workslop: 40% of desk workers got AI work needing fixes last month, about 2 hours each, in a BetterUp vendor survey.[^24][^25] Fix: the sender checks AI output before passing it on.
Shadow AI: 54% of workers would use AI tools even if not authorized.[^18] Fix: an allowed-tools list plus business plans with admin controls.[^39]

buyVsBuild.buy: Most ops teams should buy first, for standard work such as email, meeting notes, helpdesk replies and document capture.[^31][^20] Firms now buy 76% of AI use cases, say enterprise AI decision-makers polled by Menlo Ventures, an AI investor.[^31] Bought or partnered tools reached deployment about twice as often as internal builds.[^20]
buyVsBuild.build: Build when your own data or process is the edge, such as a pricing rule, a scheduling limit or a quoting method. Gartner warns many agent products are relabeled tools, so a build on a proven model can beat a weak product.[^22] Middle path: buy the seats, then build the connection to your systems.

pickElse: The process is broken or undocumented: map and fix it first with standard process improvement, such as lean methods and written procedures. Redesign is what pays.[^16]
The work is rules-based and stable: plain workflow automation or your ERP's built-in rules may be cheaper and more predictable.[^40]
The problem is a forecast or schedule with years of history: a statistical forecasting or planning tool beats a chat assistant.[^19]
Physical labor dominates: in our analysis, hand material movers rank 678th of 785, and 88% of their job has no AI use.[^10][^11] Equipment, layout or a warehouse system matter more.

sources.name: MIT NANDA, The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025 (Jul 2025)
sources.what: MIT no longer hosts the report (its link now opens the NANDA project page, checked 26 Nov 2026); copy hosted by MLQ.ai. Sample: 52 organizations interviewed, survey of 153 leaders, and 300+ public AI initiatives reviewed. $30-40 billion of enterprise GenAI investment; 95% of organizations are getting zero return; just 5% of integrated AI pilots extract millions in value. Task-specific tools: 60% of organizations evaluated them, 20% piloted, 5% reached production. Over 80% of organizations explored or piloted ChatGPT or Copilot, and nearly 40% report deployment. External partnerships with customized tools reached deployment about 67% of the time vs about 33% for internal builds: 2x as likely, twice the success rate. Only 40% of companies purchased an official LLM subscription; workers at over 90% of companies surveyed use personal AI tools for work. For mission-critical work, 90% of users prefer humans. Enterprises, defined as firms with over $100 million in annual revenue, lead in pilot count but report the lowest pilot-to-scale conversion. Read 26 Nov 2026.

offer.heading: Find the one ops workflow where AI pays first
offer.body: Your top 2 workflows ranked, and a one-page plan you can hand your CEO. Bring one workflow your team, site or unit runs every week. We'll show where AI helps, who checks its output and what to measure in the first 90 days.

reviews.notes: Would forward the one-page brief as is. Stopped at the own-data table: a bare 0.408 meant nothing, so the column now reads 'AI help score (rank of 785 jobs)' and the note defines 'a lot' as 0.40 or more. Liked that the scheduling, assigning and directing rows show no AI use; it matches how the team actually runs.

Step flows name a role on every line and fit a phone. Tripped on 'QA lead' and 'AP lead'; now 'Quality lead' and 'accounts payable lead'. Stats sources spelled out (NBER, Census survey name). Wanted the 90-day timing visible; the recipes answer line now gives four weeks of baseline and six of pilot.

Runs one site, so wanted to know the offer works for a unit, not the whole firm; the offer body now says team, site or unit. The price-the-lift step ties gains to annual pay from BLS, which is the P&L language a GM reports in. No other changes.

Read as a customer service lead and a controller. Both sign-off bullets match how they would run it, and the no-auto-send rule for 90 days is right. Asked that the workslop figure carry its vendor label in the watch-outs too, as it does in the test steps; fixed.

Bottom line is five short bullets he can read in a minute. Wanted a total, not just a per-seat price, in the brief; the cost line now says 15 users for 90 days is under $1,000 at list price, with connection work extra. No Zavient price requested or added, per Russell's 26 Nov rule.
